summary: Extends the Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) from RFC 4119 to describe moving objects, with elements for orientation, speed and heading. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Describing not just where something is, but where it is pointing and how fast it moves.

questions: what is the pidf-lo dynamic element
how is heading expressed in pidf-lo
what units does pidf-lo speed use
subtitle: Three small XML elements that let a location report say which way something faces, how fast it moves and where it is heading.

tldr.problem: The Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) says where something is at one moment, but not how it is oriented or moving.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5962 adds a Dynamic element to PIDF-LO that can hold orientation, speed and heading elements, with angles in degrees and speed in meters per second.
tldr.outcome: Receivers that do not understand the extension can ignore it, while others can track or extrapolate movement. The extra data also raises the privacy stakes.

today: RFC 5962 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Location Needs Motion
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO, defined in RFC 4119) carries the geographical location of a presentity: a physical location at a given instant. RFC 5491 extends it and gives implementers extra guidance.

RFC 5962 adds spatial orientation, speed and heading. The RFC gives two example uses. An application that continuously tracks a presentity can use velocity to extrapolate positions between measurements, and a shipping company can monitor delivery truck speed to check that speed limits are observed.
sections.eli5: A photo shows where a car was. Adding its speed and direction tells you where it is probably going next.

sections.title: Presentity and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC uses the term presentity, as defined in RFC 2778, for the device subject to location determination. The reuse of the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) comes from the similarity to presence concepts and the abstract location privacy architecture in RFC 4079.

The document does not distinguish human from non-human objects, so both are in scope. It uses the RFC 2119 key words such as MUST and MAY in the usual way.
sections.eli5: A presentity is just whatever is being tracked, whether it is a person, a phone or a truck.

sections.title: The Dynamic Element
sections.content:
RFC 5962 defines one new element, <Dynamic>. It MAY appear without any other location information. When it goes with the presentity's instantaneous position, it MUST be in the same <location-info> element as the matching geodetic or civic location. A recipient that does not support the specification can safely ignore it.

It holds three optional components. <orientation> is the direction the object is pointing. <speed> is the scalar part of velocity, in meters per second. <heading> is the directional part of velocity. Any of them can be left out when no information is available.
sections.eli5: There is a box with three slots: which way it faces, how fast it goes and which way it travels. Any slot can stay empty.

sections.title: Angles and Coordinate Systems
sections.content:
Dynamic locations assume the coordinate reference systems that RFC 5491 allows: the two-dimensional WGS 84 system urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4326 or the three-dimensional one, urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4979.

<orientation> is the direction of facing and <heading> is the direction of travel. Each holds one or two angles in degrees, which can be negative and, if two are given, MUST be separated by whitespace. They are relative to the presentity's current position.

The first angle is horizontal, measured from North toward East, so zero means North. The second angle, if present, is the elevation from the local horizontal plane. If it is omitted, the vertical part is unknown, and with one angle on <heading> the <speed> holds only the horizontal component. Appendix A gives formulas for the North and Up unit vectors in Earth Centered, Earth Fixed coordinates.
sections.eli5: The first number says how far you turn from North toward East. The second says how far up or down you tilt.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The first example has <orientation> of -3 12, <speed> of 24 and <heading> of 278. The RFC describes this as a presentity roughly facing North at a slightly elevated angle, travelling 24 meters per second to the West.

The second example is a bike travelling 12 meters per second, with its position given as a circle. The RFC says a receiver may use the speed to adjust the uncertainty over time.
sections.eli5: One example is a car heading west fast. The other is a bike whose speed helps you guess how its position fuzziness grows.

sections.title: The XML Schema
sections.content: The schema in Section 4 uses the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:geopriv10:dynamic. A <Dynamic> element is a sequence of optional orientation, speed and heading elements, followed by any number of elements and attributes from other namespaces. speed is an xs:double. The direction type is a list of doubles with a minimum length of 1 and a maximum of 2.
sections.eli5: The schema is the rulebook that checks the box is filled in correctly. It also leaves room for other people to add their own extra slots.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says no further privacy or security measures are necessary beyond those in RFC 4119. It also warns that dynamic information may be used by attackers to anticipate the future location of a presentity, so including more information in a PIDF-LO does increase the severity of an information leak.

Those who deploy location-based services are strongly advised to give users ways to control who sees their location information.
sections.eli5: Knowing where you are going is more revealing than knowing where you are, so this information needs extra care.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA is asked to register the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:geopriv10:dynamic and the XML schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:pidf:dynamic, following RFC 3688.
sections.eli5: The names used in the format get written in an official list so nobody else reuses them.

items.title: orientation
items.text: The direction the object is pointing (direction of facing).

items.title: speed
items.text: Scalar rate of change in position, in meters per second.

items.title: heading
items.text: The direction of travel; the directional part of velocity.
